subject: psychiatry
title: Electroconvulsive Therapy and Neuromodulation: Indications, Technique, and Safety

steps.title: Clinical Indications for ECT
steps.tx: **Definitive indications for electroconvulsive therapy** include severe psychotic depression with unyielding suicide intent, life-threatening depressive stupor or starvation, severe neuroleptic-induced malignant catatonia, acute refractory mania, and treatment-resistant schizophrenia. When rapid clinical response is paramount to save life, ECT remains the most rapidly acting and efficacious biological treatment available in modern psychiatric practice.

steps.title: Contraindications to ECT
steps.tx: **Safety considerations and ECT contraindications** identify significantly raised intracranial pressure as the only absolute contraindication, because transient spikes in cerebral blood flow and mean arterial pressure during the electrical stimulus risk fatal transtentorial or tonsillar herniation. High-risk relative contraindications include recent myocardial infarction within three months, unstable intracranial vascular aneurysms, acute pheochromocytoma, and severe retinal detachment.

right.title: Relative High-Risk Conditions

steps.title: Modern Modified ECT Protocol
steps.tx: **Modified electroconvulsive therapy technique** eliminates musculoskeletal fractures and patient terror by administering brief general anaesthesia alongside complete neuromuscular paralysis. Premedication with intravenous atropine or glycopyrrolate suppresses reflex vagal bradycardia, induction is achieved with intravenous methohexital or propofol, and skeletal muscle flaccidity is established with succinylcholine at 0.5 to 1 milligram per kilogram.

Prevents violent musculoskeletal contractions and fractures

steps.title: Electrode Placement Comparison
steps.tx: **Electrode placement in ECT** determines both therapeutic efficacy and the magnitude of post-ictal cognitive side effects. Bilateral (bitemporal) placement places electrodes across both frontotemporal regions, producing the swiftest clinical improvement at the expense of higher retrograde amnesia. Right unilateral (d’Elia) placement spares the dominant left cerebral hemisphere, substantially diminishing verbal memory disruption.

right.title: Right Unilateral (d’Elia) Placement
points: Electrodes placed on right nondominant hemisphere

steps.title: Therapeutic Seizure Parameters
steps.tx: **Adequate therapeutic seizure duration** mandates at least 25 seconds of observable peripheral motor seizure activity or 30 seconds of synchronous spike-and-wave discharge on concurrent electroencephalographic monitoring. A blood pressure cuff is inflated on an arm before succinylcholine injection (cuff technique), isolating that hand from muscle relaxation to allow visual confirmation of peripheral motor convulsions.

steps.title: Adverse Effects of ECT
steps.tx: **Cognitive side effects of ECT** include transient post-ictal delirium, headache, myalgias, and anterograde memory impairment that typically resolves entirely within two to four weeks following completion of the treatment course. Retrograde amnesia for events immediately surrounding the illness and hospitalization may persist longer, but modern brief-pulse and ultra-brief-pulse stimulus waveforms have drastically curtailed permanent cognitive deficits.

steps.title: Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation
steps.tx: **Repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation** provides a non-invasive neuromodulatory alternative for medication-resistant major depressive disorder without requiring general anaesthesia or inducing generalized seizures. High-frequency (10 to 20 Hertz) electromagnetic pulses are focused over the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC) to stimulate hypoactive corticolimbic circuits, administered in daily outpatient sessions over four to six weeks.

steps.title: DBS and Ketamine Infusion
steps.tx: **Deep brain stimulation and rapid-acting ketamine** represent advanced neurobiological frontiers for severe treatment-resistant depression. High-frequency electrical stimulation of the subcallosal cingulate gyrus (Brodmann area 25) interrupts pathological metabolic hyperactivity. Meanwhile, sub-anaesthetic intravenous ketamine or intranasal esketamine antagonizes NMDA receptors, triggering rapid AMPA activation and brain-derived neurotrophic factor synthesis to alleviate suicidality within hours.
